title: In This Fantasy Football League, Wine Is the Prize
summary:
Want to get your oenophile friends into football? Just add wine.

The post In This Fantasy Football League, Wine Is the Prize appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Every September, millions of people enthusiastically sign up for a fantasy football league. In this months-long game of pretend, participants role-play as owners and managers of fake football teams composed of actual players in the NFL, whose real-world performances in real-world games determine how many points are awarded to each contestant in the fantasy league. 

It is—or rather can be—a lot of fun. But very quickly after the start of each season, participants realize that they’ve accidentally adopted a second job. Suddenly there are waiver wires to monitor, injury reports to decipher, Thursday night deadlines to remember, lineup changes to make, and enough group-text notifications to make you wonder whether you’ve joined a Fortune 500 board meeting instead of a friendly football league. 

For diehard NFL fans, that’s part of the appeal. For everyone else, it’s often enough to stay on the sidelines.

As the publisher of Blood Of Gods, a magazine exploring the intersection of wine and heavy metal, I’ve come to believe that some of the most interesting communities are built where seemingly unrelated passions overlap. Wine has an uncanny ability to bring people together, but pair it with another passion—music, art, or sports—and suddenly entirely new conversations begin. 

Last season, after a few years of friendly football trash talk, my friend Jess Forster, a sommelier at Waxlight Bar à Vin in Buffalo, New York, and I started wondering if there was a way to create an NFL pool that felt less like homework and more like opening a bottle with friends. We wanted a fantasy football league for people who don’t actually want to play fantasy football.

The solution turned out to be almost embarrassingly simple. 

Instead of asking everyone to manage a fantasy roster for four months, we asked each participant to contribute a bottle of wine and make one round of predictions before Week One. That’s it. 

Once the season kicked off, there were no weekly picks to submit, no roster changes to agonize over, and no forgotten deadlines to derail your season—just football, wine, and the slow satisfaction of watching your predictions either age beautifully or spectacularly fall apart.

The result was so much fun that we immediately realized we’d stumbled onto a format worth sharing, one that could easily be replicated by anyone with a tasting group, wine club, workplace, or just a handful of friends.

Start with One Bottle

The only buy-in is a bottle of wine. 

It doesn’t have to be rare or expensive. The goal isn’t to impress anyone. It’s simply to build a prize pool that everyone would genuinely be excited to win. Some people brought dependable everyday favorites while others reached into the cellar for something they had been waiting for an excuse to open.

By kickoff, the growing collection of bottles had become an event unto itself. Familiar labels sat beside cult wines, local producers mingled with bottles from across the country, and people were already circling the wines they’d love to take home. Before anyone had earned a single point, we’d unintentionally assembled one of the most eclectic bottle shares imaginable. 

Our league included thirty participants, which meant thirty bottles of wine waiting at the finish line for our lucky winners.

Make Your Picks—Once

To keep things approachable, we built a simple Google Form that participants could complete in about five minutes. 

The form asks for each participant’s predictions for who will win the AFC and the NFC (the American Football Conference and the National Football Conference, the two major halves that make up the NFL—you know, the National Football League); who will go head-to-head in the Super Bowl; who will become the Super Bowl champion, as well as their Wild Card teams. (Sure, this takes a bit of research, but it’s easy enough to complete the form with a glass of wine in hand.) 

Once everyone clicks “submit,” the picks are locked for the season. That’s the entire commitment. Seriously.

From that point forward, all that’s left to do is watch the standings unfold. Even people who couldn’t name three quarterbacks suddenly found themselves checking division races three months into the season because, somehow, they had skin in the game.

Keep the Scoring Simple

One of the biggest lessons we learned is that simplicity wins.

It’s tempting to create elaborate scoring systems, but resisting that urge keeps the pool welcoming to casual fans.

We awarded one point for every correct division winner, one point for each correctly predicted Wild Card team, two points for each Super Bowl participant, and three points for correctly picking the eventual champion. 

One of our favorite discoveries was how little maintenance the league required. Aside from the occasional leaderboard update or check-in with the group, the season largely takes care of itself, allowing everyone to simply enjoy watching their predictions slowly rise—or collapse. There was no spreadsheet fatigue, no midseason drop-off and no one asking, “Wait…am I supposed to be doing something this week?”

Winner Takes (Most of) the Wine

Our favorite format was “winner takes most.”

With thirty bottles in the pool, first place received eighteen bottles, second place took home eight, and third place claimed the remaining four.

It struck a nice balance. The top finishers went home with an enviable haul, while spreading the prizes across three places kept more people invested until the very end.

Keep It Interesting

One thing we discovered quickly is that even though the picks never change, and most of the scoring naturally unfolds as the postseason arrives, people still enjoy having little moments of interaction throughout the season. 

Our first amendment to the league was a Best Team Name competition, roughly a third of the way into the season.

Predictably, as a group of participants that come largely from the wine world, we were incapable of resisting terrible puns. Names like Cab Sauv Your Ass, The Brutal Bruts, and a few Brettanomyces jokes made the rounds, but the eventual winner was Pfalz Start, a name that somehow managed to delight both the football crowd and the wine geeks. The winner earned two bonus points for the clever appellation after a community vote.

Later in the season, we held another vote for the bottle everyone most wanted to win. Surprisingly it became almost as competitive as football itself. In our inaugural season, the runaway favorite was a Hermann J. Wiemer Blanc de Noirs 2012 with a ten-year disgorgement. Its owner also earned two bonus points.

Neither award had anything to do with football, yet both became some of the season’s liveliest debates.

Keep the Conversation Going

Although no one had to submit anything after Week One, a few occasional updates helped keep the momentum alive.

We celebrated the participant whose improbable Super Bowl prediction suddenly looked brilliant. We commiserated with the unfortunate soul whose championship matchup was mathematically eliminated before Halloween. For your game, you might even share a leaderboard every few weeks if you feel like it.

If you really want to lean into the wine theme, have a little fun with featured games. Bills versus Ravens? Reach for Cabernet Sauvignon and prepare for controlled violence. A rainy Seahawks afternoon practically screams for Oregon Pinot Noir. Chiefs versus Eagles? Open Champagne—you’ll probably need something celebratory regardless of the outcome.

The pairings don’t have to make perfect sense. They’re conversation starters, and that’s the point.

Foster the Community

What surprised us most wasn’t how competitive the pool became. It was the wonderfully unexpected mix of people who embraced it. 

One participant had recently moved to the Northwest and, by their own admission, knew literally nothing about the NFL. They followed college football, but the pro game was another planet. So in the spirit of embracing a new home, they chose the Seahawks to go all the way. 

Months later, after Seattle won the Super Bowl, that same newcomer—and NFL newbie—came in third place, walked away with a stash of stunner bottles, and the kind of accidental bragging rights that no amount of preseason research could have guaranteed.

Friends who had never watched an entire football game suddenly found themselves following playoff scenarios. Wine professionals who disappear into harvest each autumn could still participate without having to remember weekly deadlines. Partners who normally rolled their eyes at fantasy football suddenly had a reason to cheer on Sunday afternoons.

As Forster puts it, “I think humans in general want and sometimes even ache for community. When you can connect with other wine enthusiasts or professionals through the lens of sports or music or other topics, it’s so fun.” 

The format also remains intentionally low lift, allowing people to be as involved—or uninvolved—as they want to be throughout the season.

This isn’t just a football pool. Football is simply the framework. It could be literally anything else—basketball, Formula 1, RuPaul’s Drag Race. 

The real reward is creating another reason for people to gather, laugh, exchange a little friendly trash talk, and stay connected throughout a season, particularly the fall and winter. It’s a reminder that wine has always been at its best when it brings people together, and that sometimes all it takes is another shared passion to make that happen.

If your tasting group, office, or family has been looking for a new tradition this fall, consider this fantasy-football-league-but-with-wine your blueprint. Collect a few bottles, pour a glass, lock in your picks before Week One, and let the season do the rest. 

You might walk away with eighteen bottles of wine or zero. But if our experience is any indication, you’ll also walk away with a tradition everyone is already looking forward to repeating before the next kickoff.

title: Wine Grapes Are Thriving In One of the Driest Places On Earth
summary:
Over the last two decades, winemakers have been flocking to Chile’s Atacama Desert for its distinct and vibrant character.

The post Wine Grapes Are Thriving In One of the Driest Places On Earth appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When you step off the plane in Copiapó, the gateway to Chile‘s Atacama region, the vast, dusty landscape makes you wonder how a single vine could survive here—let alone thrive. 

The answer lies in the transverse valleys that stretch from the Andes Mountains to the Pacific Ocean, flourishing even alongside and within the Atacama, the world’s driest non-polar desert. Cooling coastal breezes, rivers, and temperature shifts at higher altitudes make viticulture possible in this seemingly inhospitable landscape. 

Since the 16th century, locals in the northern Huasco, Elqui, and Limarí Valleys have cultivated grapes primarily for Pisco. Over the last two decades, however, wine producers have begun exploring this area, known as Norte Verde (which translates to Green North).

Wines made here are vibrant and fresh, with a distinct character that sets them apart from those of Chile’s central valleys. This isn’t a passing trend but an emerging expression of Chilean wine built on a shared commitment to premium, low-intervention, terroir-driven winemaking.

Huasco Valley: Freshness in the Atacama Desert

In 2010, Ventisquero Wine Estates planted its first vines in the Huasco Valley, a remote region on the southern border of the Atacama Desert where few producers had previously ventured. 

“Even there, in the driest desert on earth, the Pacific Ocean and the Camanchaca fog bring freshness and balance to the vineyards,” says Horacio Fuentes, Ventisquero’s export director.

The estate’s vines grow just 13 miles from the coast, and despite its location, the valley is not hot. Thanks to the sea, average annual temperatures range from 62°F to 66°F, and the Huasco River ensures water is readily available, too.

The range of soils includes sandy loam and clay with varying salt content, but it’s the limestone that defines the valley’s character.

“What surprises people most about these wines is not their power, but their elegance and freshness,” Fuentes says. “You get purity, tension, minerality, and natural acidity.” 

Ventisquero’s goal is to make wine that reflects its origin. Winemakers achieve that end with a low-intervention approach, employing native yeast and aging in untoasted foudres or cement eggs, and avoiding filtering before bottling.

The Elqui Valley: Vineyards that Scrape the Stars

At the edge of the Atacama Desert, the picturesque Elqui Valley is renowned for its Pisco production. But it’s also an emerging region for delicious wines with dramatic tension.

Agriculture in Elqui follows the Turbio River from the Andes Mountains to the Pacific Ocean. Wine producers tend to prefer higher elevation areas of over 7,000 feet, where the vines grow on granite, clay, and silt soils, and diurnal temperature shifts caused by high altitude and clear skies allow the grapes to fully mature.

“Making mountain wine limits you in many ways, but the grape quality is unique,” says Viñedos de Alcohuaz winemaker Rosario Fillol. “You get intense concentration, excellent natural acidity, and vibrancy.” Here, winemakers celebrate the incredibly distinct landscape, and are genuinely committed to terroir and a clear regional identity.

“Producers in the Norte Verde respect the land and work with less conventional winemaking approaches that reflect the region in the glass,” adds Fillol. 

Her team stomps grapes barefoot in granite lagares made from mountain rocks, seeking a softer extraction for an enhanced tannic structure. They also utilize concrete eggs and amphorae to allow micro-oxygenation without imparting flavors, so the Elqui character shines through.

Limarí Valley: The Power of Limestone and Ocean Influence

The Limarí valley is in the Coquimbo region next to the Atacama, and its top vineyards are located near the Pacific Ocean. This coastal influence lowers temperatures, reduces sunlight, and brings morning fog and higher humidity. As a result, grapes here ripen slowly, which is crucial for delicate varieties like Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

But growing vines in Limarí is not easy. In some areas, that coastal influence can complicate things, leaving plants needing protection from the strong ocean breezes, and producers like Tabali having to blend aquifer water with river water to reduce salinity before irrigating.

Chardonnay, in particular, greatly benefits from Limarí’s terroir. Utilizing the region’s limestone soils, which provide wines with exquisite vibrancy, winemakers can maximize the grape’s unique flavor profile.

“Limarí Chardonnay tends to show a more restrained aromatic profile, less intense and less fruity, with a distinct flavor expression,” says Felipe Müller, CEO and chief winemaker at Tabali. The wines are “sometimes slightly saline, with a chemical balance that sets it apart from other cool-climate regions in Chile.” 

Seeing the success of Limarí’s wines, powerhouse labels like Santa Rita and Amelia (Concha y Toro) have started to source grapes and produce wines in the region. These bottlings can be bright and flinty or focused and elegant, but all express the Valley’s signature mineral characteristics.

Additionally, a growing focus on premium wines has been key in establishing the northern valleys as a quality wine region.

“There are few wineries in this area, and the overall quality level is significantly higher compared to the Central Valley and other regions with many producers,” says Müller. “This has been crucial in quickly establishing many of these wines among Chile’s top offerings.” 

In a relatively short time, wines from Huasco, Elqui, and Limarí have developed strong identities that express and surpass the extreme climate where the vines grow. Winemaking in Chile has never been easy—but it’s never been more exciting, either.

title: Why ‘Quality Over Quantity’ Is Good for the Wine Industry
summary:
Consumption may be down, but open-mindedness and willingness to spend is up.

The post Why ‘Quality Over Quantity’ Is Good for the Wine Industry appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Chris Liu believes that there’s a bright side to shorter bar tabs. 

“People are drinking less in terms of quantity, but I find them more discerning in terms of quality,” says the beverage director of Bloomsday, a wine bar and restaurant in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. “They’re very intentional about what they buy.”

The practice extends beyond Bloomsday’s barstools. People of all ages, appetites, and tax brackets are recalibrating their consumption habits and redefining value at the bar and bottle shop—and it could have a big impact on wine. Whether that’s a positive development depends on your outlook and how much time we all have. 

As countless headlines and Reddit threads will tell you, modern wine businesses face an array of evolving social, economic, and environmental challenges. But the drink-less-but-better movement isn’t an existential threat. It’s proof that many people who are cutting back are still interested in wine and eager to make the most out of every glass or bottle they try. 

Armchair analysts who bemoan generational shifts and elegize consumption data tend to ignore this crucial detail: People who are drinking wine are doing so more skillfully and thoughtfully than ever before. That’s not a silver lining so much as lightning in a bottle. The only question is whether there’s enough time for it to ignite.

Curiosity Takes Center Stage

“There’s been a steady evolution in the way people drink wine,” says Jamie Ritchie, the managing director of international auctions at Berry Bros. & Rudd in Washington, D.C. In previous decades, many collectors would purchase multiple cases from known regions or producers without investigating their preferences or looking beyond the usual suspects. 

These days, “people are more curious and willing to experiment,” he says. “The curiosity goes across generations. There’s a gravitation at all levels and at all ages for people to understand a bit about what they’re drinking and get excited about different things.” 

Chase Sinzer agrees. The owner of Claud, Stars, and Penny in New York City has observed a sea change in the ways people approach wine lists. In the 2010s, guests at restaurants where he worked would come in and say, “‘I know what I want, and it’s going to be Bordeaux or Brunello, and I’d like to spend this amount of money, and I don’t want anyone to talk to me,’” he recalls. “That same person now goes, ‘Can you please give me a few options? I can’t wait to hear what you have to say.’”

Ritchie links some of the open-mindedness and exploratory zeal to the effects of the pandemic. During shutdowns, many people studied wine. When hospitality businesses reopened, they shed their sweatpants, went out to bars and restaurants, and were eager to taste everything that the wide world of wine had to offer. Like their customers, retailers experienced these discovery trends, too.

Better, Not More

This same time period coincided with an enduring emphasis on moderation over excess. “Everyone is drinking less, for health reasons or generally for interest in living a more balanced life,” says Ritchie. 

That’s not a death knell, either. It’s a call to action. When someone is more knowledgeable and curious about what they drink, they can investigate each purchase to tailor it to their tastes and budgets. These are prime conditions to create lasting relationships with wine—ones with more long-term benefits than intermittent, happy-hour binges.

This all presents an opportunity for sommeliers, salespeople, and other wine professionals to meet people where they are and cultivate their curiosity. It’s a chance to learn from and avoid the knee-jerk anti-Merlot or Anything But Chardonnay sentiments of previous eras that led many folks to write off entire categories or wine itself without a second thought (or glass). “We’re making up for previous sins of sommeliers of different generations now,” Sinzer says.  

Besides, in the current economic moment, few of us are sitting on mountains of surplus cash to throw at lackluster wine. Trading multiple mediocre glasses for something you really love aligns with the way many people spend. They might be willing to shell out a few extra dollars for one great glass or bottle from a producer who shares their values, if consumer behaviors in fair-trade coffee, organic produce, and thrifted versus fast fashion are any indication.  

A quality-over-quantity mindset creates new and better points of access to wine, Liu says. “People are willing to spend $15 on something good and only have one bottle that night, rather than spend $15 on a case of poorly made beverages without thinking about it,” he says. “That’s actually helping the industry in a lot of ways because you have a new entry to the market that’s not garbage.”

Meaningful change takes time, and many grape growers, winemakers, and retailers need the market to rebound yesterday. But wine is a long game, too. After 8,000 years, how we think about, make, and drink it continues to evolve. Even if you only have one pour on any given night, that glass is still half-full.

title: Why ABV Is Showing Up on Cocktail Menus
summary:
These days, drinkers can cut back on their alcohol intake with increasing precision.

The post Why ABV Is Showing Up on Cocktail Menus appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • American alcohol consumption is at a record low, which is driving a rise in low-proof options.
  • Some bars now list abv on menus to help consumers decide what to order.
  • Transparency in drink strength improves hospitality, promotes inclusion, and helps businesses sell more lower-abv beverages.

As evidenced by our current era of mini martinis and tiny cocktails, zero-proof drinks, and low-proof spirits, the trend persists: Everyone is drinking less. 

A 2026 Gallup poll reports that though the share of Americans who say they drink alcohol is at 54%—a record low for this annual survey that has been conducted since the end of Prohibition.  More and more people are exploring non-alcoholic options or simply reducing the number of glasses they have with dinner. These days, drinkers can even cut back on their alcohol intake with increasing precision.

In the same way that nutritional data like calories and grams of protein started appearing on menus, a growing number of cocktail lists around the country are displaying a drink’s abv (alcohol by volume). The trend allows bartenders and owners to give their cocktails—and alcohol levels—deeper levels of consideration and intention at all stages, from recipe development to marketing.

A Tool for Discovery

According to Kraig Rovensky, partner and beverage director at Life on Mars in Seattle, local drinkers are already accustomed to seeing abv info on menus because of craft beer culture. At Life on Mars in Seattle, the espresso martini is listed at 20% abv, while the Pathfinder Spritz is at just 0.03%. Since the bar’s opening in 2019, the menu has always listed each item’s abv, Rovensky says, because he wants guests to feel confident about what they order and not worry about mistakenly getting something that’s too strong for them. 

“Most people don’t know how different the alcohol content is in vermouth versus whiskey,” Rovensky says. “I’ve heard from people they were shocked at how much alcohol was in an Old Fashioned versus a spritz. As beverage professionals, this is obvious to us, but I think we forget just how little the general consumer knows.” 

Stuart Jensen, owner of Peach Crease Club in Denver, believes that offering abv information to guests is a natural extension of hospitality. It’s a way to guide and educate guests, empowering them with the intel they need to become savvy bargoers each time they order a Guinness (4.2% abv) or an Old Fashioned (44.9% abv). 

“It’s not something that everyone notices or takes into consideration, but those that do are very appreciative,” Jensen says. “And the staff is happy to have one more tool that helps them point guests in the direction of a drink they’ll enjoy.” Declaring abv percentages also helps bar teams educate customers unfamiliar with rare or unusual spirits and drinks. The Hellenic restaurant MEZŌ Mediterranean in Dedham, Massachusetts, serves Greek beers like Fix Hellas and Mythos and traditional spirits like ouzo and tsipouro, with which guests may be unfamiliar. 

Co-owner and executive chef George Panagopoulos says that adding abv information to MEZŌ’s menu has given diners another point of reference. “It helps set expectations and makes people feel more confident trying something new,” he says. “Guests appreciate the transparency and the information often sparks conversations with our team about Greek drinking culture and the stories behind these beverages.” 

Louis Lin, the chef and owner of Xiao Ye in Portland, Oregon, was thinking about both approachability and the bottom line of his business when considering adding the abv info to his drink menu. His wife and business partner, Jolyn Chen, is not a big drinker, he says: “She’s always been really aware of whether wine lists and cocktail menus feel approachable to someone who doesn’t drink.” And so he began to view the practice of listing abv percentages, whether for his gin-based Italo Disco at 27% or the Pandan Coconut Sparkler at 0%, as an invitation to those who don’t drink or drink less to find something they might enjoy. Moreover, it helps the business’ bottom line. 

“If a diner gets stuck with a super-boozy drink they can’t finish, there’s a chance they won’t order another,” Lin says. “But if they end up drinking and loving something that’s 12%, maybe they’ll be inclined to get another knowing that they won’t overdo it.”

Mixing and Matching on the Menu

At the buzzy new restaurant Oriana in New York City’s Nolita neighborhood, zero-abv cocktails are listed alongside the rest of the main menu. The non-alcoholic Ghost Flame with black tea, pepper, and NA amaro sits right next to the mezcal-centric Smoking Sol with an abv of 20%, rather than being relegated to a separate, perhaps less-loved section. 

“We put just as much thought and development into those drinks,” says Oriana’s owner and sommelier Cedric Nicaise. This subtle difference makes the low- and no-abv offerings feel just as intentional and significant as every other cocktail they serve, he explains, and guests “appreciate having that information available and the way it’s presented.”

As a trend, listing the alcohol content on menus is likely to stick around. As a statement on how we drink and dine today, it’s all quite fitting. Much like how these low- or no-abv tipples are just as well crafted as spirit-forward heavy hitters on menus, drinking less or not drinking alcohol is just as valid a vibe as tossing back martinis with urbane swagger. As ever, information is power and gestures of inclusion are meaningful—in both life and cocktail menus.

title: These Wineries Are Just as Serious About ‘Merroir’ as They Are Terroir
summary:
In places like the Chesapeake Bay, winemakers and seafood purveyors are bridging the gap between land and water in pursuit of a common goal.

The post These Wineries Are Just as Serious About ‘Merroir’ as They Are Terroir appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
On a cool November evening on Virginia’s Eastern shore in the Chesapeake Bay, a small but bustling crowd gathers around wine and oysters.

Tables are topped with plates of the freshly shucked bivalves, and each adult sips a glass of wine. The scene, framed by the Bay glittering in the background and rows of trellised grapevines rustling in the wind, depicts a typical weekend at the Chatham Vineyards tasting room from November to March. The collaborative event, called “Winter Wine and Oyster Weekend,” is the perfect showcase of “merroir.” 

Coined in the early 2000s, the term “merroir” is the water version of terroir: it refers to when surrounding marine elements impact the flavor profile of marine life. Just as wine has terroir, oysters have merroir. And in places like the Chesapeake Bay, the largest United States estuary (a mostly encapsulated large body of water in which fresh water meets seawater), winemakers and seafood purveyors are bridging the gap between land and water in pursuit of a common goal: building a more sustainable environment while nurturing the local economy.

What Goes Better Than Wine and Oysters?

From a flavor perspective, oysters and wine make natural companions.

Chatham Vineyards, whose vines are just 300 yards away from the oyster beds, has been hosting its wine and oyster pairing events for 17 years. The winery’s steel-fermented, minimal intervention Chardonnay, one of its most successful bottlings, is a stalwart in its consistency of product and ability to pair with Chesapeake Bay oysters.

“There is a unique minerality in the wine that counters the salinity of Chesapeake Bay oysters, while a ripe fruit component matches the sweetness of the oyster,” says John Wehner, Chatham Winery’s owner.

About 15 miles north of Chatham Winery lies Laughing King Oyster Company and Vessel Farm Winery. Owners Thomas and Erin Haney founded the oyster company first and then established the vineyard less than a mile from the oyster beds, with the intent of pairing the wine with the oysters. As Thomas puts it, “the focus is small-batch production with high quality” that offers a full spectrum of the Eastern Shore flavor profiles, like salinity, umami, and minerality. 

While over 50 grapes were initially planted in the vineyards, Vermentino is emerging as the highlighted wine for the oyster pairing, which “has been a way to introduce a grape most people are not familiar with,” says Thomas.

The Dog and Oyster Micro Vineyard, located further north, has hosted wine and seafood events for 15 years. Like Chatham Winery, they offer a Chardonnay that is fermented in stainless steel to preserve the freshness and minerality to pair with the oysters.

Protecting the Bay with Merroir and Terroir

Aquaculture and oyster farms are vital to the Chesapeake Bay estuary. Estuaries are known for their brackish water—the mix of fresh and saltwater—that nurtures the ideal environment for organisms like oysters to grow. That set of conditions is mutually beneficial: a full-term oyster is capable of cleaning 50 gallons of water a day. The mollusks also lower the carbon footprint by utilizing carbon in the formation of their shells, and they further aid in lowering oxygen depletion by consuming algae, thus minimizing dead zones in the water.

In terms of flavor, bodies of water like the Chesapeake Bay promote the balance of saltiness (from the seawater) and sweetness (from the silt bottom and fresh water) that makes oysters delicious. It is only fitting that a region that is ramping up its wine production fosters a union with a product unique to this environment.

While there are some 250 commercial aquaculture enterprises in the Chesapeake Bay, many of the wineries are not part of an established wine trail. These unique “merroir/terroir” experiences in this region invite and inform a sustainable path forward for both wine and oysters.
